title: OpenSSL Patches 14 Security Flaws Including High-Severity Memory Disclosure Bug
content_md: OpenSSL has released security updates addressing 14 vulnerabilities across its TLS, DTLS, QUIC, X.509, CMP, and cryptographic implementations, including a high-severity out-of-bounds read that could disclose heap memory to a remote DTLS peer. The most severe issue, tracked as CVE-2026-84782, affects DTLS handshake retransmission handling in OpenSSL 4.0, 3.6, 3.5, 3.4, 3.0, 1.1.1, and 1.0.2. The flaw occurs when a DTLS handshake message write is suspended because the underlying transport cannot accept additional data, while the retransmission timer simultaneously attempts to resend a previously queued handshake message. OpenSSL Patches 14 Security Flaws OpenSSL’s retransmission code reused buffer and position-tracking data associated with the handshake message that was still being written. Instead of resetting the retransmitted message’s read position to its beginning, the operation could start at the offset where the suspended write stopped. This condition could cause the server or client to send leftover data from another, potentially larger handshake message as plaintext DTLS handshake content. In certain circumstances, the operation could read beyond the allocated message buffer, exposing heap-resident data to the remote peer. If the read reaches unmapped memory, the affected application may crash instead, causing a denial-of-service condition . The vulnerability has been assigned CWE-125, an out-of-bounds read weakness.
